danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Efter fyrst Andrej kom Boris hen for at byde Natasja op, derefter adjudanten, der havde åbnet ballet, og adskillige andre unge mænd, så hun — rødmende og lykkelig, idet hun overrakte sine overflødige kavallerer til Sonja — ikke holdt op med at danse hele aftenen. Hun hverken lagde mærke til eller så noget af det, der optog alle andre. Ikke alene undlod hun at bemærke, at kejseren talte længe med den franske ambassadør, og hvor særlig nådig han var mod en vis dame, eller at fyrst Den-og-den og Den-og-den gjorde og sagde dette og hint, og at Hélène havde stor succes og blev æret med særlig opmærksomhed fra Den-og-den, men hun så ikke engang kejseren og bemærkede kun, at han var gået, fordi ballet blev mere livligt efter hans afsked. Under en af de muntre kotilloner før soupeeren var fyrst Andrej atter hendes partner. Han mindede hende om deres første møde i alléen ved Otradnoje og om, hvordan hun ikke havde kunnet sove den måneskinsnat, og fortalte hende, at han uvilkårligt havde overhørt hende. Natasja rødmede ved den erindring og forsøgte at undskylde sig, som om der var noget at skamme sig over i det, fyrst Andrej havde overhørt.

Som alle mænd, der er vokset op i selskabet, nød fyrst Andrej at møde nogen, der ikke tilhørte den konventionelle selskabstype. Og det var Natasja med sin overraskelse, sin begejstring, sin generthed og endda sine fejl, når hun talte fransk. Med hende opførte han sig med særlig omhu og ømhed, sad ved hendes side og talte om de enkleste og mest ubetydelige ting; han beundrede hendes sky ynde. Midt i kotillonen, efter at have afsluttet en af figurerne, vendte Natasja, stadig forpustet, tilbage til sin plads, da en anden danser valgte hende. Hun var træt og pustende og tænkte tydeligvis på at afslå, men lagde straks sin hånd muntert på mandens skulder, idet hun smilede til fyrst Andrej.

»Jeg ville gerne sidde hos dig og hvile: jeg er træt; men du kan se, at de bliver ved med at byde mig op, og jeg er glad for det, jeg er lykkelig og elsker alle, og du og jeg forstår det hele,« og meget, meget mere sagdes i hendes smil. Da hendes partner forlod hende, løb Natasja hen over gulvet for at vælge to damer til figuren.

»Hvis hun går til sin kusine først og derefter til en anden dame, bliver hun min kone,« sagde fyrst Andrej til sig selv, ganske til sin egen forbavselse, mens han betragtede hende. Hun gik først til sin kusine.

»Sikke noget vrøvl, der til tider falder én ind!« tænkte fyrst Andrej, »men hvad der er sikkert, er, at den pige er så bedårende, så original, at hun ikke vil danse her en måned, før hun er gift... Sådanne som hende er sjældne her,« tænkte han, mens Natasja rettede en rose, der var ved at glide af hendes livstykke, og satte sig ved hans side.

Da kotillonen var forbi, kom den gamle greve i sin blå frakke hen til de dansende. Han indbød fyrst Andrej til at besøge dem og spurgte sin datter, om hun morede sig. Natasja svarede ikke straks, men bare så op med et smil, der bebrejdende sagde: »Hvordan kan du stille det spørgsmål?«

»Jeg har aldrig moret mig så meget før!« sagde hun, og fyrst Andrej lagde mærke til, hvor hurtigt hendes tynde arme løftede sig, som for at omfavne sin far, og øjeblikkeligt faldt igen. Natasja var lykkeligere, end hun nogen sinde havde været i sit liv. Hun var på det lykkens tinde, hvor man bliver fuldstændig god og venlig og ikke tror på muligheden af ondskab, ulykke eller sorg.

Ved det bal følte Pierre for første gang sig ydmyget over den position, hans kone indtog i hofkredsene. Han var mørk og fraværende. En dyb fure løb hen over hans pande, og stående ved et vindue stirrede han over sine briller uden at se nogen.
På vej til soupeeren kom Natasja forbi ham.
Pierres mørke, ulykkelige ansigt slog hende. Hun standsede foran ham. Hun ønskede at hjælpe ham, at skænke ham noget af overfloden af sin egen lykke.
»Hvor det er dejligt, greve!« sagde hun. »Ikke sandt?«
Pierre smilede fraværende og forstod tydeligvis ikke, hvad hun sagde.
»Jo, jeg er meget glad,« sagde han.

»Hvordan kan nogen være utilfredse med noget?« tænkte Natasja. »Især en så prægtig fyr som Bezukhov!« I Natasjas øjne var alle mennesker ved ballet lige gode, venlige og prægtige, der elskede hinanden; ingen af dem i stand til at krænke en anden — og derfor burde de alle være lykkelige.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew, Boris came up to ask Natasha for a dance, and then the aide-de-camp who had opened the ball, and several other young men, so that, flushed and happy, passing off her extra partners to Sonya, she danced without stopping all evening. She noticed nothing of what occupied everyone else. Not only did she fail to see that the Emperor had a long conversation with the French ambassador, or that he was especially gracious to a certain lady, or that Prince So-and-so did this and So-and-so said that, or that Helene was a great success and received special attention from Such-and-such — she didn't even see the Emperor, and only realized he'd left because the ball became livelier after his departure. During one of the merry cotillions before supper, Prince Andrew was her partner again. He reminded her of their first meeting in the avenue at Otradnoe and how she had been unable to sleep that moonlit night, and told her how he had accidentally overheard her. Natasha blushed at the memory and tried to excuse herself, as if there had been something to be ashamed of in what Prince Andrew had overheard.

Like all men who have grown up in society, Prince Andrew enjoyed meeting someone who didn't conform to the standard social mold. And such was Natasha, with her surprise, her delight, her shyness, and even her occasional mistakes in French. With her he was especially careful and tender, sitting beside her and talking about the simplest and most trivial things, admiring her shy grace. In the middle of the cotillion, having completed one of the figures, Natasha, still out of breath, was returning to her seat when another dancer chose her. She was tired and panting and clearly thought of declining, but immediately put her hand gaily on the man's shoulder, smiling at Prince Andrew.

"I'd love to sit beside you and rest — I'm tired; but you see how they keep asking me, and I'm glad of it, I'm happy, and I love everybody, and you and I understand all of it" — and much, much more was said in her smile. When her partner released her, Natasha ran across the room to choose two ladies for the figure.
"If she goes to her cousin first and then to another lady, she will be my wife," said Prince Andrew to himself, quite to his own surprise, as he watched her. She did go first to her cousin.

"What nonsense sometimes enters one's head!" thought Prince Andrew. "But one thing is certain — that girl is so charming, so original, that she won't be dancing here a month before she'll be engaged... Girls like her are rare here," he thought, as Natasha, readjusting a rose that was slipping on her bodice, settled down beside him.

When the cotillion ended, the old count in his blue coat came up to the dancers. He invited Prince Andrew to visit them and asked his daughter if she was enjoying herself. Natasha didn't answer at once but only looked up with a smile that said reproachfully: "How can you even ask?"

"I have never enjoyed myself so much!" she said, and Prince Andrew noticed how her thin arms rose quickly as if to embrace her father and instantly dropped again. Natasha was happier than she had ever been in her life. She was at that peak of bliss where one becomes completely kind and good and cannot believe in the possibility of evil, unhappiness, or sorrow.

At that ball Pierre felt for the first time humiliated by the position his wife occupied in court circles. He was gloomy and distracted. A deep furrow ran across his forehead, and standing by a window he stared through his spectacles, seeing no one.
On her way to supper Natasha passed him.
Pierre's gloomy, unhappy expression struck her. She stopped in front of him. She wanted to help him, to share the overflowing abundance of her own happiness.
"How wonderful it is, Count!" she said. "Isn't it?"
Pierre smiled absently, clearly not grasping what she had said.
"Yes, I'm very glad," he said.

"How can anyone be unhappy about anything?" thought Natasha. "Especially such a fine person as Bezukhov!" In Natasha's eyes all the people at the ball were equally good, kind, and wonderful — people who loved one another, none of them capable of hurting anyone else — and so they all ought to be happy.
